record_reviews.summary: Blyth’s 23 February 1856 Calcutta letter is a long, authorial incoming ALS. It begins with four printed copies and instructions for Darwin’s distribution, then moves through Asiatic Society grievance and museum prospects, a botanic-garden holiday, Gallus varius and hybrid fowl, pigeon and macaw/marmoset supply, Arabian asses, deer and canine-hybrid fertility, a dead wild dog, Coracias skins, and distributional bird comparisons. The text distinguishes Blyth’s remembered authorities and proposed experiments from observations, and its apparatus identifies the missing earlier letter and Darwin’s abstract. The supplied 23 February date is XML-bounded to that day; sender Blyth and recipient Darwin are explicit. No direct Darwin prompt survives in this source.

record_reviews.summary: Blyth’s March 1856 notes are a composite authorial letter: an opening discussion of fowl and pigeon nomenclature, Annobon and Arabian birds, Squatarola, Gallus hybrids, and the musk-ox skull; a large pigeon section describing Indian races and proposed crosses; an explicit ‘March 22’ later section about dark feet in wild versus tame pigeons; a further argument that asses are African and a separate discussion of hemippus, onager and related forms; and a newspaper extract on horned cattle. The apparatus says the first part predates 22 March and the completed letter is later, while the marginal Squatarosa sentence has no indicated placement. XML bounds are 22 March 1856. No Darwin answer or complete prompt is preserved here.

record_reviews.summary: Blyth’s 3 April 1856 notes transcribe David Scott’s difficult left-handed account of Indian pigeon names and breeds, preserving a long numbered sequence including Runts, Fantails, Tumblers, Carriers and Nuns. Blyth then compares Scott’s observations with his own, checks Dixon and Temminck, infers possible livia/intermedia origins from rump colour, proposes Egypt, Turkey and Syria for comparative collections, and returns to guinea-fowl distribution and domestication. The text explicitly marks Scott’s quoted voice and Blyth’s interpolations; the apparatus identifies Scott and Blyth’s abstract. XML’s date is based on Darwin’s annotation. This is source context, not an answer to a surviving Darwin letter.

record_reviews.summary: Blyth’s 8 January 1858 letter asks whether zebra striping artificially applied to a jackass might affect its offspring and proposes analogous experiments. It reports a Bengal jungle-fowl lacking the usual cheek-lappet, frizzled fowls, references Blyth’s Indian bird articles, and records the celebratory arrival of Lucknow garrison with a strongly editorialized comparison of European and Asiatic forces. The date is taken from Darwin’s annotation and the apparatus notes that the letter’s opening/other source context is incomplete; no Darwin prompt or answer is present. Blyth is the XML sender to Darwin.

The source is only three body blocks, with the supplied date in an excluded/header layer and apparatus about Thompson and Darwin’s hybridism annotation. It establishes dispatch and an observation, not receipt or a surviving Darwin question.

record_reviews.summary: Wells’s 17 November 1858 letter forwards beans and gives their history: White Tick beans from B. S. Stanhope, no visible first-year sport, a large second-year crop of changed beans, and a report that the third generation ‘turned out all manner’ after presumed bee intervention. He says the beans retain vitality and that he will sow some himself. The footnote identifies this as a response to Darwin’s Gardeners’ Chronicle inquiry about bee crossing; the sender is Wells and recipient Darwin, dated 17 November. The source is a complete three-block ALS, but it does not contain the missing public inquiry itself.

record_reviews.summary: Wells’s 25 November 1858 follow-up answers a specific missing Darwin question about whether the first- or second-year beans grew near other varieties. He cannot fix the first-year distance beyond 100 yards, but says the second-year plants were almost certainly beside Longpods and Mazagans and notes 8–12 bee hives each season. The letter is a complete three-block ALS from Wells to Darwin dated 25 November, but its apparatus says Darwin’s question is not found and only identifies it as evidently responding to the 17 November Wells letter. That evidence supports a scoped missing-prompt boundary, not a 2363-to-2374 incoming-letter pair.
